p1: A stair is the most familiar thing in Venice. There are hundreds of bridges, and every one of them is a stair. This autumn the studio built one that goes nowhere: seven steps, set into the corner of two white walls, rising to a landing that leads to nothing but the wall above it.
p2: It is called Seven Steps to Heaven. Standing in front of it in Tesa 41, one of the team put the idea in a sentence: “I think that the ultimate point of a sculpture like this is that, being devoid of points of reference, you fill it with yourself.”
h2.drawing: A drawing with a question on it
p3: It began as a pen drawing. A corner, two walls ten feet high, a floor ten feet by eight, and inside it a stair of seven steps, each twelve inches high and thirty-six inches wide, climbing to seven feet. Three feet of wall are left above the top step. Under the title, a note in pencil asks the question that the next months would keep asking: check how high is each step?
fig.sketch: 7 Steps to Heaven. Pen and pencil sketch, with dimensions
p4: The drawing has a history. A notebook page from the summer is full of steps cut into blocks: stairs sunk into a cube, stairs climbing between two volumes. At the bottom, a note to Aram: “let us see what AI can come up with, inspired and related to these drawings.” The stair against the wall came out of that conversation between hand drawings and the computer.
fig.notebook: Notebook page: steps cut into blocks, with a note to Aram
p5: A stair is two numbers: how high each step rises and how far each tread runs. Change them and the same seven steps become steep and urgent or low and ceremonial. The studio modelled the work nine times, and tested ten proportions of rise to run, from shallow to almost a ladder, before settling the version shown here.
p6: Version nine was rendered from eight cameras placed around it. These are renderings, not photographs: they show the design, with a grey stair inside white walls.
fig.front-right: Seven Steps to Heaven, version 9, three-quarter front from the right. Rendering
p7: Walk around it and it changes character. From the front it is a stair. From above it is seven bands. From behind there is no stair at all, only the outside of a corner.
p8: Then the model was placed in the hall where it would be made. Rendered into photographs of Tesa 41, against the brick and the pilasters of the Arsenale, it becomes a piece of architecture: a room inside a room. Again, these are renderings, not the finished work.
p9: In October the drawing became an object. The pieces were carried along the water and through the doors of the Arsenale by hand, as everything is in Venice, then skimmed, sanded and painted white in the studio.
fig.quay: Carrying a section of the stair along the water
fig.door: Through the door, one flight at a time
p10: While they worked, the team talked about what they were making. “Humans are surrounded by cubes,” someone said. “I was thinking about the obsession of us, as humans, creating these shapes.” Another called it a viaggio, a trip: “There is a start, there is a finish, but the finish is not so clear.”
p11: And another went further: “I think it’s like a life. You have a past, you have a story, you have a future, but you are in the present, and you know only the present.”
fig.table: Zadik Zadikian and the team at the table, with the small models
p12: Zadik, a hand on the top step, put it most plainly: “These steps are not taking you anywhere, physically. It just takes you some place, mentally, or emotionally. It’s another form of function.”
p13: The stair is chosen because everyone already knows it. “You see it everywhere, but in Venice you see it every second. Immediately you say: it’s a stair. There is familiarity. That familiarity is easy to accept. As if I know it: you feel comfortable.” The familiar form is the way in. What happens on the other side is up to the viewer.
p14: Which brings it back to scale. Seven steps fit inside a room ten feet wide, and yet: “It creates something that doesn’t materially exist, but that can be even bigger than the sculpture you’re seeing. Because I can see here the climb to heaven in a relatively small space, I can see something that is immensely large, that makes me feel immensely small.”
p15: Seven Steps to Heaven is in the studio at Tesa 41. Stand at the bottom and look up.
